Session 3 includes quiet, overlapping workshop conversation, especially around 01:00-01:14; its automatic text is often unclear and must not be treated as reliable quotations. Unclear room chatter is not used as evidence in the study guide.

pages.title: Day 2: what matters
pages.subtitle: 500 Eurasia B11 | Three recordings, one study guide | 4 hours 44 minutes condensed

blocks.title: The day in one sentence
blocks.body: Earn a useful conversation, establish whether there is a real buying opportunity, and use AI to multiply a well-defined process rather than automate confusion.

blocks.title: 1. A reply is not a qualified buyer
blocks.body: An interested person may have no urgent problem, no route to approval, or no ability to buy. Define the evidence that earns a prospect more of your time.

blocks.title: 2. Relevance beats a bigger email list
blocks.body: A real observation about the buyer's situation, one useful insight, and one small question work together. Generic praise, feature lists and empty follow-ups do not establish value.

blocks.title: 3. Discovery comes before persuasion
blocks.body: Understand the actual process, the cost of the problem, why it matters now, and how a decision gets made. Leave with a scheduled next step or an honest reason not to proceed.

blocks.title: 4. AI-native is an operating model
blocks.body: Mikheil Nadareishvili describes three layers: copilots for everyone, coding agents for builders, and agents that complete whole processes. All three depend on usable company knowledge and clear controls.

blocks.title: The most important MediMind implication
blocks.body: Your free parallel system is a strong offer, but a weak qualification test by itself. Before building, agree on the hospital's problem, reviewers, success test and decision date. Otherwise you may deliver free work without moving a buying decision.

Fast path: this page → hospital gate (p. 4) → messages (p. 7) → call script (p. 9) → action checklist (p. 17). The separate transcript PDF preserves the full recognized speech; this guide removes repetition and classroom administration.

blocks.title: One shared deck, not three different decks
blocks.body: The morning and afternoon Airtable records point to the same 83-slide discovery/qualification deck. The lunch session points to a separate nine-screen HTML presentation. Duplicate links have been consolidated.

blocks.title: What the assignment asks you to produce
blocks.body: A defined SQL; outreach based on one ICP and its value proposition; a discovery-call script; a practiced call assessed with a scorecard; and reasons/next steps for unqualified leads. Building an outreach workflow is optional homework.

blocks.title: How to interpret these notes
blocks.body: Lecture takeaway means a paraphrase of the recordings or decks. MediMind application means a proposed adaptation, not something the lecturer said about your company. Reported statistics remain attributed examples, not independently verified benchmarks or MediMind results.

Source references use S1, S2 and S3 for recordings and D1/D2 for the two decks. D1 slide numbers are printed on the slides; D2 refers to displayed screen order. Approximate rewatch times are navigation aids, not exact quotation boundaries.

pages.title: Qualify the opportunity
pages.subtitle: Lecture takeaway | S1 00:15-00:32; S3 opening | D1 slides 5-12, 51-63

rows:
ICP
Ideal customer profile
The specific kind of company and buying situation you can serve well.
A broad industry such as 'healthcare'.

MQL
Marketing-qualified lead
A lead meeting your agreed observable fit/engagement criteria; ready for a qualifying conversation.
Traffic or form fills with no relevant fit.

SQL
Sales-qualified lead
Conversation has established the problem, fit, buying context and realistic reason to move forward.
A demo request, friendly reply or enthusiastic product feedback.
Opportunity
A qualified potential purchase with a next step, an estimated deal value and a reasoned projected close date.
Every lead in the database multiplied by an imagined contract value.

blocks.title: BANT and ANUM ask the same essential questions
blocks.body:
BANT: Budget, Authority, Need, Timing.
ANUM: Authority, Need, Urgency, Money.
Use them as things to learn, not an interrogation in a fixed order. A previous purchase suggests spending capacity; it does not prove money is available now.

blocks.title: Discover the approval process, not someone's status
blocks.body: Instead of asking whether someone is 'the decision-maker', ask how this type of purchase is approved, who else participates, and what each person needs to see. A supportive contact may be valuable without being the final signer.

blocks.title: Learn from your worst customers too
blocks.body: List what made customers difficult to serve: missing integrations, unsupported requirements, excessive custom work or an unsuitable process. Turn those lessons into explicit fit criteria before another salesperson repeats the mistake.

blocks.title: The trade-off
blocks.body: A tempting one-off customer can absorb engineering and support time without advancing the product you want to sell repeatedly. Qualification protects both sales time and delivery capacity.

pages.title: MediMind's hospital gate
pages.subtitle: Proposed application | A free evaluation still needs a qualified hospital and a decision process.

blocks.title: Working SQL definition
blocks.body: A hospital in our serviceable market with a confirmed operational problem we can address, a named internal sponsor, a credible approval and purchasing path, and an agreed next step toward a time-bounded evaluation.

headers: What a useful answer looks like
rows: Problem + impact
One recent example; who does the extra work; frequency; time, cost or revenue at risk. Treat assumed pain as a hypothesis until the hospital confirms it.
Fit + feasibility
The relevant workflow is supported, required dependencies are understood, and no known requirement makes the proposed evaluation unsuitable.
Sponsor + approval route
A person willing to coordinate reviewers; the clinical/operations, IT/security and purchasing participants are identified.
Timing + buying path
A real reason to evaluate now, likely approval steps, current relevant spend and a review date. Free testing does not remove future purchasing constraints.
Mutual next step
Both sides agree who will do what by when. The next conversation is scheduled, not merely promised.

blocks.title: Before allocating a free build
blocks.body: Agree the specific evaluation scope, a baseline and success test, hospital reviewers, the data/security arrangements, and what decision follows the review. Do not count verbal enthusiasm as technical readiness.

blocks.title: Four milestones that must stay separate
blocks.body:
Qualified opportunity → a credible buyer/problem.
Access and evaluation prerequisites ready → work can safely begin.
Parallel system ready → MediMind has delivered the testable environment.
Evaluation completed → hospital reviewers have tested it and recorded a decision.

Recommended primary learning metric remains new hospitals beyond the anchor partner completing a defined parallel-system evaluation. Review weekly and report a rolling 28-day count. Access granted, delivery, acceptance and a paid agreement are separate measurements. This reporting window is a proposal, not a lecture-mandated deadline.

pages.title: Outreach that earns a reply
pages.subtitle: Lecture takeaway | S1 00:32-01:02 and 01:16-01:38 | D1 slides 13-25, 35-45

blocks.title: The job of the first message
blocks.body: Get the next useful response. Do not try to sell the whole company, explain every feature and secure a meeting in the same paragraph.

rows: Choose one buyer and the issue that matters to that role.
Send the same copy to the CEO, IT lead and clinical lead.
Use a real business signal and explain why it matters.
List personal facts, generic praise or irrelevant research.
Offer a useful observation, a specific example or evidence.
Lead with your biography, funding or a long feature list.
Use short, simple language and one easy question.
Ask for a demo, feedback, an introduction and a contract at once.
Build genuine familiarity through relevant channels.
Pretend to know someone or invent a previous conversation.
Add fresh value in a follow-up.
Repeat 'just checking in' or guilt the person for not replying.

blocks.title: The message changes with the person
blocks.body: A sales leader may care about an immediate pipeline target; an engineer may care about implementation risk. For MediMind, an introduction to a hospital CEO and a technical follow-up to its IT lead should support the same sale but answer different questions.

blocks.title: Use AI for preparation, retain human judgment
blocks.body: The lecturer criticizes generic AI-written outreach and recommends actual research and human rewriting. The transferable lesson is to verify context, relevance and tone—not to treat a broad statement about what AI can or cannot do as a permanent technical fact.

Lecture examples included personalized videos, useful research, event connections and gifts. For MediMind, prioritize relevant professional introductions and helpful material; do not copy invasive personal targeting, invented familiarity or gift-based pressure.

pages.title: Examples, numbers and judgment
pages.subtitle: Lecture evidence, not promises | S1 00:53-01:01, 01:16-01:41, 01:57-02:11 | D1 slides 21-23, 36-47

blocks.title: Why the better examples worked
blocks.body:
Visible problem: a search screenshot showed a prospect something concrete about competing ads.
Unexpected insight: an aviation company replaced a technology introduction with analysis of the recipient's routes.
Relevant proof: a short peer example connected a result to a problem the recipient recognized.
Live workshop lesson: a reference logo only helps if the buyer recognizes it; lead with the buyer-relevant result, and do not stack a meeting request and a pilot request in one first message.

rows: Cold-email replies: 3-6%; top performers 10-15%
Lecture comparison figures, not a forecast for Georgian hospital CEOs.
Cold-email meetings: 0.2-2%; 50-80 words per first touch
A reminder that outreach must be concise and conversion measured. The best length still depends on context.
LinkedIn InMail replies: 10-25%
A different channel and audience; not directly comparable with warm hospital introductions.
Example adding LinkedIn: replies 3% to 11%
A case example, not proof that adding the channel will produce the same lift for MediMind.

blocks.title: Resolve the apparent contradictions by testing
blocks.body: Some slides favor adding a note to a connection request; another example favors a blank request. One case deliberately accepts fewer connections to get better replies. These are different tactics, not universal rules. Optimize for qualified conversations and completed evaluations, not acceptance rate alone.

blocks.title: Email infrastructure is supporting work
blocks.body: The lecture covers sender authentication, mailbox setup, sending volume, list hygiene and unsubscribes. Do not treat its exact tool choices, warm-up tactics or limits as verified provider policy. MediMind's immediate bottleneck is targeted hospital conversations, not building a high-volume email machine.

blocks.title: Your weekly review
blocks.body: Count the hospitals contacted, relevant replies, discovery calls held, qualified opportunities, and evaluations completed. Log the reason for every stalled lead. Keep channel and audience separate so a warm-introduction result is not mixed with cold email.

pages.title: Three messages you can adapt
pages.subtitle: MediMind application | Drafts only—nothing has been sent. Replace brackets with verified details.

blocks.title: 1 · Ask a connector for a useful introduction
blocks.body: Hi [Name] — who at [Hospital] owns the problem of staff repeating work between disconnected systems? MediMind builds a parallel alternative for the hospital to test for free, before any purchase commitment. If this is a current priority for them, would you be comfortable introducing us to that person?

blocks.title: 2 · First message to the hospital leader
blocks.body: Hi [Name] — [specific, verified reason this may matter now]. Is your team still entering the same information into different systems? We can build a free parallel MediMind environment so your team can compare an alternative without replacing the system they use today. No purchase commitment before you test it. Would a short conversation about where the repeated work happens be useful?

blocks.title: 3 · Follow up with a concrete evaluation idea
blocks.body: One way to make this comparison useful: pick a workflow your team finds frustrating, record how it works today, then run the same steps in the parallel system. You can judge the time, missing information and handoffs for yourselves. Which workflow would you want us to prove first?

blocks.title: What to prepare as believable proof
blocks.body: A short, permission-cleared demonstration of the chosen workflow; a clear evaluation plan; and any customer evidence whose scope you can substantiate. Until measured hospital results are available, offer a test instead of inventing a percentage improvement.

blocks.title: Where the price-match offer belongs
blocks.body: Use it once the hospital understands the comparison and you have verified the scope, duration and remaining availability of the 'next 10 clients' offer. Do not state an unverified number of remaining places or imply free evaluation means no security, data or implementation agreements.

Keep the broad AI vision for a relevant follow-up: explain what can be demonstrated today and what is a future capability. In the opening message, the urgent problem and the tangible test should be easy to understand without an AI lecture.

pages.title: A discovery call is a decision
pages.subtitle: Lecture takeaway | S3 first 47 minutes | D1 slides 51-78

blocks.title: The purpose
blocks.body: Find out whether advancing is useful for both sides. A discovery call is not a generic demo and not an opportunity to pitch over every answer.

rows: 1 · Frame the call
One-sentence context; confirm time and agenda; agree what decision the conversation should enable.
2 · Map current work
How the process actually runs, tools and people involved, the trigger, the workaround and what good looks like.
3 · Deepen the problem
A recent example; frequency; the effect on time, money, risk or morale. Confirm quantities rather than assuming them.
4 · Understand constraints
Competing priorities, deadlines, evaluation process, required capabilities, approvals and purchasing path.
5 · Decide and schedule
Summarize what you heard. Propose a next step that addresses it, or explain why not to proceed. Book the next conversation while together.

blocks.title: Listen for the next question
blocks.body: The lecture suggests roughly 40% talking and 60% listening. Treat that as a coaching cue, not a pass/fail formula. Follow the buyer's answer, dig into specifics, and avoid turning your script into a checklist read aloud.

blocks.title: One call or two? Set expectations first
blocks.body: The discussion allows discovery and a demo in one call for a simple, transactional sale. A complex sale may benefit from a separate, prepared demonstration with the right stakeholders. Explain that plan beforehand. If your CTA says 'Book a demo', do not surprise people with an unexplained qualification-only call.

blocks.title: The weak-answer trap
blocks.body: 'Our process is chaotic' is a starting point, not qualification. Ask about the last occurrence, who was involved, what happened next, and the consequence. An honest 'we do not know yet' is better than filling the gaps with industry averages.

pages.title: Your hospital discovery script
pages.subtitle: MediMind application | Matches the exact question categories in D1 slide 78 | Suggested 25-minute call

blocks.title: Opening / framing
blocks.body: Thanks for making time. MediMind connects hospital work in one system. I'd like to understand one process that causes trouble today, who would need to evaluate an alternative, and whether a free parallel comparison would be useful. We have 25 minutes—is that still right?

blocks.title: Two current-state questions
blocks.body:
1. Could you walk me through the last time this workflow crossed departments, from start to finish?
2. Which systems and people were involved, and what did staff have to do manually?

blocks.title: Two pain / impact questions
blocks.body:
3. Where did information go missing, get entered again, or hold up the next person?
4. How often does that happen, and what does it cost in staff time, delayed billing or other measurable consequences?

blocks.title: Two urgency / timing questions
blocks.body:
5. What makes this worth addressing now rather than later?
6. By when would you want an improvement, and what other priority could delay the decision?

blocks.title: Two authority / process questions
blocks.body:
7. Who would need to test, approve and sign off on a change like this?
8. What would each of those people need to see in a parallel evaluation before supporting the next step?

blocks.title: One budget question
blocks.body: 9. What do you spend today on the systems involved, and how would funding for an alternative be approved if the evaluation showed enough value?

blocks.title: One next step
blocks.body: 10. If we agree the workflow, success test and data/security requirements, can we schedule an evaluation-planning meeting with [sponsor], [operations/clinical reviewer] and [IT lead] for [date]?
Do not ask all ten mechanically. Follow answers, confirm your understanding, and note unknowns. Do not promise an automatic two-week clock before prerequisites and delivery scope are agreed.

pages.title: Score the evidence, not the vibe
pages.subtitle: Lecture scorecard adapted for MediMind | D1 slides 64-66, 79 | Mark Yes / Partial / No

rows: Current state understood
The process, systems, people and workaround—not just the name of a department.
Pain confirmed
A recent example described by the hospital, and the people who experience it.
Impact measured
A frequency, time/cost estimate or other agreed baseline; distinguish measured values from estimates.
Urgency established
Why now; a target decision window; what could displace the project.
Buying path understood
Sponsor, reviewers, approvers, signer, funding route and unresolved procurement requirements.
Fit and constraints checked
Required workflow, dependencies and any known blocker; do not score an unknown as a yes.
Next step mutually agreed
Action, owner and date for each side, with the next meeting scheduled.

blocks.title: What the lecture's contrasting calls demonstrate
blocks.body: In the recruiting example, the strong call uncovers a real process and concrete time/cost figures. The weak call hears 'chaotic', pitches features and never establishes impact. At S3 00:44-00:54, the lecturer adds: founders need enough call skill to coach and assess salespeople. Practice, review actual conversations, and keep recurring objections and useful responses in a shared playbook.

blocks.title: After-call recap template
blocks.body:
You want to improve: [workflow/problem].
Today: [baseline and source; unknowns clearly marked].
A useful comparison would show: [agreed test].
People involved: [names/roles].
Next: [hospital action + owner + date] and [MediMind action + owner + date].
Review meeting: [date/time].
Please correct anything we misunderstood.
Proposed operating rule: do not approve a free custom build on a total score alone. A missing sponsor, required approval, safe evaluation arrangement or agreed review must be resolved explicitly.

pages.title: Three practice calls, three lessons
pages.subtitle: Lecture workshop | S3 about 01:17-01:44 | Role-play examples, not real customer results

rows:
Recruitment agency
01:17-01:26
The seller offered tool consolidation and fewer invoices. The buyer rejected the invoice problem and wanted better candidate search.
Do not defend an assumed pain. Ask which outcome the buyer actually needs and how current tools fall short.

Personal trainer
01:26-01:34
The seller described an attractive dashboard and asked the buyer to imagine using it. The discussion did not establish urgency, purchasing context or a next step.
Avoid leading the buyer toward your solution. An interesting product conversation is not yet a qualified opportunity.

Motorcycle importer
01:34-01:43
The expected topic was dealer support; the buyer shifted to market expansion and asked several questions about what the seller could do.
Clarify which problem matters most, explain the relevant scope briefly, then return to useful discovery. Do not continue down a script for the wrong problem.

blocks.title: Customer interview versus sales discovery
blocks.body: An interview primarily helps you learn about a customer and their work. Sales discovery also establishes whether there is a current buying opportunity: a problem worth solving, fit, urgency, a buying path and a mutually agreed next step. Do not mistake learning something interesting for moving a sale forward.

blocks.title: A phrase to practice - MediMind adaptation
blocks.body: 'I can show you how that works. First, which issue would make the biggest difference for your team? Then I can show the comparison that matters to you.' Answer relevant questions honestly; ask permission to return to discovery rather than dodging them.

blocks.title: The actual closing homework
blocks.body: Practice navigating a call, not just writing good questions. Use a teammate who can challenge assumptions or change priorities. Review with the scorecard, then prepare the next demo around the ICP and problems uncovered in discovery. The lecturer also offered call feedback and office-hour practice at the time of the session.
For MediMind: 'many disconnected systems' is a starting hypothesis. Find the specific consequence this hospital wants changed, and make that the purpose of the parallel evaluation.

pages.title: A useful no still moves you forward
pages.subtitle: Lecture takeaway + MediMind routing proposal | S3 disqualification section | D1 slides 67-75, 80

rows: No urgent priority
Record the future trigger and agree whether/when to reconnect. Send only relevant material; remove it from the active forecast.
Wrong hospital or use case
Explain the mismatch. Close as not a fit; refer elsewhere only if you genuinely know a suitable option.
Required capability missing
Log the requirement. Reconnect if the capability becomes available; do not sell an invented roadmap or deadline.
No sponsor / approval route
Ask for the right introduction or a joint call. Keep it as qualification incomplete until the buying path is understood.
No credible purchasing path
Clarify the budget cycle and decision trigger. A free trial alone does not establish future willingness or ability to buy.
Evaluation not feasible yet
Identify the technical, data, security or staffing dependency and its owner. Do not start a delivery countdown.
No response
Use a bounded, relevant follow-up sequence, then pause. Silence is not proof that the hospital is intrinsically a poor fit.

blocks.title: Simple routing flow
blocks.body:
Fits and ready? Schedule the next evaluation step.
Fits but not ready? Record the missing condition and a re-entry trigger.
Does not fit? Close honestly.
Not enough information? Keep qualifying—do not force a yes or no.

blocks.title: Graceful language
blocks.body: 'It sounds as though this is not the priority to push right now. If [trigger] changes, would it be useful to reconnect around [date]?' Or: 'The workflow you need is outside what we can support today. I do not want to promise a fit we cannot deliver.'
Store the reason, date, owner and next trigger in one prospect record. Repeated reasons should feed back into targeting, product priorities and the definition of a qualified hospital.

pages.title: What an AI-native company does
pages.subtitle: Lecture takeaway | Mikheil Nadareishvili, Chief Analytics Officer, Bank of Georgia | S2 opening; D2 screens 1-6

blocks.title: Not just buying AI subscriptions
blocks.body: The model has to be part of how people work, how builders produce things and how whole processes get completed. Company knowledge is the shared foundation.

rows: 1 · Copilots for everyone
People in different roles use AI during everyday work.
Choose the task, provide context and check the output.
2 · Builders with coding agents
Developers and analysts delegate more implementation and analysis work.
Define the result, review changes and test quality.
3 · End-to-end agents
A process can run through several steps, using tools and escalating exceptions.
Set authority and limits, handle exceptions and remain accountable.
Foundation · knowledge
Rules, definitions, examples and working context are available to the system.
Maintain trustworthy, current, permission-appropriate sources.

blocks.title: Why the starting point matters
blocks.body: The bank has established processes, existing systems and many employees and customers. The speaker contrasts the cost of changing those habits with a startup's ability to design its work around AI from the beginning.

blocks.title: Five founder principles, in plain language
blocks.body:
1. Make AI useful and accessible across roles.
2. Treat organized knowledge as something you build and maintain.
3. Test whether an agent can do a defined job before adding capacity.
4. Redesign the whole process, not just a slow step.
5. Put permissions, supervision and safeguards in place from the start.
The 'agent before the next hire' principle is the speaker's provocation, not a claim that all jobs should be automated. The deck also emphasizes human judgment and intervention where needed.

pages.title: Results and the context lesson
pages.subtitle: Speaker-reported examples, not independently audited results | S2 about 00:06-00:14; D2 screens 4-7

rows: 63% daily AI use among back-office staff; about 100 ambassadors and 400 internal assistants
Adoption is an organizational effort, not just distribution of a tool.
6,600 hours freed per month; +31% IT throughput in 2025
Important qualification: at about 00:07 the speaker calls the hours-saved figure a vanity metric and says it is hard to measure reliably.
2-3x analytics productivity; 10x experiments
More capacity can support more experiments as well as faster delivery. Measurement methods are not established in this guide.
72% of customer chats resolved without a person, in Georgian, as of August 2026
Bounded processes can be delegated with human escalation.
Text-to-Sale: 2x usual conversion; about 1% added to loan/deposit sales
Using existing interactions as context for a subsequent action.
Call-quality pilot: audit all interactions versus about 4% manually
A pilot example, not a claim that every bank workflow is fully autonomous.

blocks.title: The same model can perform very differently
blocks.body: The deck cites a DoorDash data-agent example: on a 100-question comparison, 73% correct with business context versus 48% with the same tools but without it. It separately describes a broader improvement from 43% to 90%; these are different comparisons, not one continuous three-step experiment.

blocks.title: The knowledge loop
blocks.body: Everyday work generates evidence → AI drafts a useful knowledge update → a responsible person reviews it → approved knowledge improves future work. The quality and maintenance of that context are part of the product.

Sources named by the deck include Bank of Georgia, DataIQ, Lion Finance Group's 2025 report, and DoorDash's 'Inside Vera, DoorDash's Data Agent' (16 September 2026). They are references cited by the speaker; this pack does not independently validate their statistics.

pages.title: AI Q&A: beyond the slides
pages.subtitle: Lecture takeaway | S2 00:17-00:47 | Practical detail added in the room

rows:
Adapt the process or replace it?
00:17-00:19
For hard-to-replace systems such as a data warehouse, document non-negotiable constraints and teach the agent to work with them. Redesign other processes when that is more practical.

What makes adoption work?
00:21-00:26

Find genuinely motivated internal users, train them to help colleagues, and work with the people who understand each domain. Security, legal and other control teams need to collaborate, not arrive only at the end.

How long did it take?
00:23-00:25

He describes at least six months for the chatbot and roughly six to eight months for broad staff adoption, despite a strong existing AI team. These are that bank's experience, not general implementation targets.

Who owns AI-written work?
00:26-00:30; 00:34-00:35
Responsibility stays with people directing and reviewing it. Staff should read and understand the work; important systems can require an additional reviewer.

How do you choose a new model?
00:40-00:43
Test representative tasks from the actual domain. Compare quality with the existing model, including regressions. Newer is not automatically better for every task.

How do you keep agents controlled?
00:15-00:16; 00:40-00:41
Use the minimum permissions needed, simple designs, evaluation tests, monitoring and alerts. A convincing demo is not sufficient evidence for a business-critical process.

Build or buy?
00:35-00:38
Specify what the system must do before evaluating vendors. The bank described a detailed requirement set, including control over access and cost.

How do you control tool cost?
00:31-00:33
Match spending to usage: occasional users and intensive builders need not have the same arrangement. Exact vendor economics were not established here.

blocks.title: MediMind implication
blocks.body: Keep your milestones honest: preparing a parallel environment, a hospital completing an evaluation, a production migration and validated AI workflows are different achievements. A fast first demonstration should lead to a controlled next step, not imply that all later work is already complete.

The speaker also emphasizes managing expectations: a striking creative AI demonstration does not prove competence in finance or another specialized workflow. Apply the same distinction to hospital administration and clinical work.

pages.title: Apply AI-native thinking to MediMind
pages.subtitle: Proposed application—not a claim about current product readiness or clinical effectiveness.

blocks.title: The strongest connection to your product vision
blocks.body: Connected hospital work creates a place to maintain useful context. That can support better AI workflows—but a unified database alone does not establish safe or effective clinical autonomy.

blocks.title: Start with your own team's repeatable work
blocks.body: Use approved source material to prepare hospital briefs, draft follow-up notes, identify unanswered qualification questions, and assemble evaluation plans. Keep a person responsible for factual accuracy, promises and anything sent externally.

rows: Customer evidence
Known pains, buyer language, confirmed constraints and permitted references—with sources and dates.
Product truth
What can be demonstrated today, what is in testing, what is planned, and what is not supported.
Commercial rules
The actual price-match terms, evaluation scope, delivery prerequisites and capacity limits.
Evaluation playbook
Baseline, test steps, reviewer roles, success criteria, failure cases and review/decision process.
Reusable lessons
After each evaluation, record what failed, what was learned and which knowledge should change.

blocks.title: Then define one bounded agent job
blocks.body: Example: after a discovery call, draft a qualification record, flag missing evidence and prepare a follow-up email. A human approves the record and sends the message. Measure accuracy, correction effort and useful next steps before expanding responsibility.

blocks.title: For hospital-facing AI, keep the claims precise
blocks.body: Separate administrative assistance, clinical decision support and any proposed autonomous action. Each needs its own evidence, controls and accountable owner. The bank's experience does not demonstrate medical safety or guarantee improved patient outcomes.

Practical guardrail: use only data approved for the workflow and system; do not place patient records into general-purpose sales or knowledge tools. This pack does not authorize new access, integration or automated actions.

pages.title: Your assignment and next actions
pages.subtitle: Lecture deliverables + proposed MediMind execution plan | D1 slides 4, 49-50, 78-80

rows: SQL definition
Hospital gate + evidence checklist
Agree it with the team.
Outreach content
Connector, leader and follow-up drafts
Choose one segment and add verified context.
Discovery script
Opening + 2 current-state, 2 impact, 2 timing, 2 authority, 1 budget and 1 next-step question
Rehearse it with a teammate.
Practice and scorecard
Yes / Partial / No evidence review
Run a role-play and change weak questions.
Unqualified flow
Reason-specific routing and re-entry triggers
Add these reasons to the prospect tracker.
Optional workflow
Research → draft → human check → outreach → reply → qualify → next step
Automate only after the manual steps are clear.

blocks.title: A small one-week plan
blocks.body:
First: choose a narrow hospital segment and review the prospect list against the gate.
Next: identify an introduction path and current problem; prepare a useful comparison idea.
Then: rehearse, hold calls and write evidence-based recaps. For evaluations already running, schedule a halfway check so there is time to correct problems before the decision (adapted from S3 00:56-00:58).
End of week: review where prospects stopped; adjust the targeting, message or next step.

blocks.title: What to track without building a complex dashboard
blocks.body: Hospital, source/connector, sponsor, current stage, confirmed pain, missing qualification evidence, next action, owner, due date and outcome. Separately timestamp access readiness, delivery, evaluation completion and commercial decision.

blocks.title: The test of progress
blocks.body: Could a teammate explain why this hospital is worth pursuing, what it will evaluate, who will judge the result, and what happens after that? If not, more copy or more automation is unlikely to be the next useful step.

blocks.title: What is included
blocks.body:
01: this study guide, with lecture takeaways and clearly marked applications.
02: full automatic transcripts of all three recordings in one PDF.
Transcripts: searchable TXT, timed SRT subtitles and structured JSON for each session.
Source decks: accessible D1 reference text and source links.
Working files: reusable notes, cached transcription sections and validation records.

blocks.title: Accuracy boundaries
blocks.body: All recordings are processed end-to-end, but speech recognition is not a human-verified verbatim transcript. Names, accents, cross-talk and quiet room exercises can produce errors. The guide interprets the content; use the original recording before quoting someone or relying on an uncertain number. Speaker results are not evidence of MediMind results.

Terms: CVP = customer value proposition; CTA = call to action; CRM = customer/prospect tracking system; copilot = AI assisting a person; agent = AI carrying out a defined multi-step task using tools and rules.
